body.p:
The sensible man makes peace with his enemy, if he is compelled to that: he treats him well, displays friendliness, and shows him
trust on his part-if he can’t manage otherwise-but he makes haste to get away from him when he finds
a way for that.
He also knows that he who is felled by his own candor can hardly be excused for his misstep;

he should keep his promise
to whom he enters into a truce with, while trusting himself with this in ways in which he doesn’t trust others

p.n: The Best Thing Is Distance From the Enemy

body.p:
and preferring nothing to distance from his enemy
as much as he can.

p.n: Staying Away from the Enemy is the Best Judgment

body.p: Staying away from the huntsman is prudent for you; and staying away from you is prudent for me.

p.n: The Rat Will Love the Cat from Afar

body.p:
My judgment is to like you
from afar,

p.n: The Rat Does Not Need a Reward

body.p: and there’s no duty for you to honor me likewise.

p.n: The Last Verdict Is No Reunion

body.p: There isno way for us to ever reunite.’”

The Chapter of the King and the Bird Qanbara.
It is the chapter of the people of requital and those wary of one another, which is the parable of someone who is mistrustful and not open toward
another after that which the other had done to him before. It includes the importance of developing trust and avoiding to be misled
by someone’s agreeableness and kindness. It calls for being wary, guarded, and cautious.
The King said to the Philosopher: “I have heard the parable of the man who is surrounded by his enemies; who seeks help from one of them
and reconciles with him, so that he can be delivered, through it, from that he had feared; who meanwhile keeps his promise and is saved. Present to me this next parable
of the people who should be wary from one another. The Philosopher said: “They claim that some grand king
called Ibn Madyar had a bird called Qatra, who could talk, was smart, and had a nestling.
The King ordered the bird, Qatra, and his nestling be taken to a woman who was the lady over all the women
in his palace and ordered her to take good care of him. Then the woman gave birth to a male child, who grew accustomed to the nestling
